title: Why Digits Slip Away
description: Why numbers will not stick, how chunking helps, and the runner who reached 80 digits
tryIt: Read a long number off something at home, such as a serial number, chunk it into groups of three or four with a meaning for each, and recite it ten minutes later.

concepts.title: How it works: figures form no pictures
concepts.contentHtml:
Someone reads you a twelve-digit number, once. Can you say it back? Most people lose the thread somewhere after the seventh digit, and it is not carelessness. Mark Twain put his finger on the problem in an essay for children: dates are hard to remember because they consist of figures,1 which look monotonously alike and form no pictures, so the eye gets no chance to help. A string of digits is ten interchangeable symbols with nothing to hold on to.

At Carnegie-Mellon University, the psychologists William Chase and K. Anders Ericsson found out what happens when an ordinary person refuses to accept that limit. Their volunteer, known as SF, heard random digits read at one a second and tried to say them back. He started out just like almost every untrained subject, repeating the sounds to himself. Then SF, a keen long-distance runner, started to use his knowledge of race times as a memory aid,2 and he invented his running-time code on Day 5.3 The group 3492 became "three forty-nine point two, near-world-record mile time".4 Groups that could not be times became ages: 896 can't be a time because the second digit is too big,5 so it became 89.6 years old, a very old man. Others became years, so 1943 was near the end of the Second World War.

By the time the team reported it in Science in 1980, after more than 230 hours of practice, SF's span had climbed from 7 digits to 79,6 and it later passed 80.7 Their explanation had two parts: a code that turned digit groups into meaningful units, and a retrieval structure, an organised set of slots for retrieving these units from long-term memory in the right order.8 That is this whole skill in miniature: give digits meaning, then give the meanings places.

concepts.title: Drill: chunk like SF
concepts.contentHtml:
Before you learn any system, feel what plain chunking can do. Chase and Ericsson noted that for ordinary people the best group size seems to be 3 or 4 digits,1 and that SF himself never allowed more than 4 groups to be clustered together.2 So you work in small groups, and you give each one a meaning.

  1. Split. Break the number into groups of three or four digits, and avoid leaving a lonely single digit at the end.
  2. Mean something. Give each group a meaning you already own: a year, a time on the clock, an age, a price, a bus route, a house number.
  3. Link. Run the meanings together into a tiny story, so each one calls up the next.
  4. Cover and test. Hide the number, recite it, then check. Count how many groups came back in the right place.
  5. Keep your score. Write it down. In Lesson 3 every pair of digits gets its own image, and you can measure the difference.
Drill Read these eight groups once, find a meaning for each and link them, then cover them. The quiz will ask for them in order.
  1. 1943
  2. 3492
  3. 896
  4. 1230
  5. 365
  6. 999
  7. 2012
  8. 747

Notice what happened with the first three. You met them a minute ago with SF's meanings attached, and they are probably the easiest to hold. That is the effect Chase and Ericsson measured: meaning turns a group of three or four digits into one thing to remember. The hard ones are the groups you could not attach to anything, which is exactly the gap the major system will fill.

concepts.title: Myth check: a head for numbers
concepts.contentHtml:
Two popular beliefs about number memory fall over in the laboratory.

Myth Practising digit span strengthens your memory in general.
Reality SF's training stayed exactly where he put it. After three months of digit practice, Chase and Ericsson tested his span for consonants: he showed no transfer at all, and his consonant span was around 6.1 His skill was a set of digit codes, not a bigger memory.
Myth People who can hold huge numbers were born with a special memory.
Reality SF began as an average subject who, with a couple of hundred hours of practice, turned himself into a memory expert.2 Chao Lu, who set a Guinness World Record by memorising 67,890 decimals of pi,3 was studied by Hu, Ericsson and colleagues in 2009, and his digit span was only in the normal range.4 His feat rested on mnemonic encoding and thousands of hours of practice.

Wait, really? Your language changes your digit span. In 1980 N. C. Ellis and R. A. Hennelly tested people fluent in both Welsh and English. Welsh digits take longer to say than English ones, and the same people had a significantly smaller digit span in Welsh than in English. The authors traced the gap to word length, not intelligence, which also explained why Welsh children's norms on a digit span test were lower than American children's. Holding digits for a few seconds leans on how quickly you can say them to yourself.

title: The Major System
description: Ten families of consonant sounds, free vowels, and two centuries of number alphabets
tryIt: On your next walk, decode five shop signs or street names into numbers using only their consonant sounds.

concepts.title: How it works: a sound for every digit
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is a puzzle from the 1630s: how do you make 314159 memorable? Turn it into a word. Pierre Hérigone, the pen name of Baron Clément Cyriaque de Mangin,1 wrote a six-volume Cursus mathematicus that appeared between 1634 and 1642.2 In it he introduced a code by which numbers were translated into words to aid memorising them.3 His code gave digits to vowels as well as consonants, so 314159 became the word4 cadator.

Number alphabets kept being reinvented. Richard Grey published his Memoria Technica in 1730,5 and he too assigned both vowels and consonants to figures, in a way a later critic called perfectly arbitrary.6 The step that matters came in The New Art of Memory, a London book founded on the principles taught by Gregor von Feinaigle (third edition, 1813): consonants only. The consonants carry the number, like a skeleton,7 and the vowels are only the ligaments, free to be added wherever you need them to make a word.

The version you will learn reached New York in 1844, when Francis Fauvel-Gouraud lectured there and in Philadelphia.8 His printed table is, sound for sound, the code in this lesson, and his big idea was to code sounds, not letters. For the soft family of 6 (sh, zh, ch and j), he gave the credit to the French teacher Aimé Paris, calling him his brilliant contemporary.9 Psychologists call the result the phonetic mnemonic; this course uses its popular name, the major system.

concepts.title: Drill: learn the code
concepts.contentHtml:
Fauvel-Gouraud squeezed the whole code into one silly sentence, his "synthetic formula": Satan may relish coffee pie.1 Read only the consonant sounds and you get s, t, n, m, r, l, sh, k, f, p, which are the digits 0 to 9 in order.

  1. Say the formula until the ten core sounds come out in order without thinking.
  2. Hang each sound on a hook. Feinaigle's book chose letters for their shape: t has one down stroke, n has two down strokes and m has three,2 and L was the Roman numeral for fifty, so it takes 5.3 Fauvel-Gouraud added that r is the fourth letter of "four", a handwritten f looks like a stretched 8 and p is an upside-down 9.4
  3. Add the sound-alike partners. Close cousins share a digit: d joins t, z and soft c join s, v and ph join f, b joins p, hard c, hard g and q join k, and j, soft g and the zh in "measure" join sh and ch. Th counts as 1.
  4. Ignore the rest. Vowels, and w, h and y, carry no number,5 so add them freely to build words.
  5. Practise on the street. Decode words you see: "moon" is m, n, so 32; "tyre" is t, r, so 14; "pie" is 9.
Drill Learn the code. Cover the sounds, say them for each digit, then check. The quiz will ask.
  1. 1: t, d, th
  2. 2: n
  3. 3: m
  4. 4: r
  5. 5: l
  6. 6: sh, ch, j, soft g
  7. 7: k, hard c, hard g, q
  8. 8: f, v, ph
  9. 9: p, b
  10. 0: s, z, soft c

concepts.title: Myth check: letters or sounds?
concepts.contentHtml:
Most beginners trip over the same two misunderstandings.

Myth You turn a word into a number by counting its letters.
Reality You code the sounds you hear. Fauvel-Gouraud's rules: two identical letters together count once, so "matter" is m, t, r, which is 314.1 But in "accident" the two c's make different sounds, k and s, so both count. "Ocean" is sh, n, which is 62,2 because its c sounds like sh. X splits into k and s, so "box" is 970, and a letter swallowed by its neighbour drops out: in "match" the t vanishes into ch, giving 36.
Myth The code is arbitrary, so learning it just adds more to memorise.
Reality Nearly every pairing has a hook chosen on purpose: shape (one, two and three down strokes for t, n and m), history (L for the Roman fifty) and sound. Fauvel-Gouraud admitted some of his analogies were incomplete,3 but a hook takes seconds to learn and saves you hours of rote repetition.

Wait, really? Number alphabets were once a stage show. Fauvel-Gouraud describes watching Aimé Paris take questions from a packed hall for three whole hours, and insists that he did not commit the slightest error in his hurried answers.4 That is one admirer's account of a rival, so treat it as a claim, not a verified record. The copy of Fauvel-Gouraud's lectures that has been scanned for the public belonged to a famous showman: it comes from the Harry Houdini Collection at the Library of Congress.5

title: A Peg for Every Number
description: Building a 00 to 99 list of images, and what experiments found about learning one
tryIt: Write your own words for 00 to 19 tonight, then test yourself tomorrow with ten random pairs from that range.

concepts.title: How it works: one image per pair
concepts.contentHtml:
The code turns digits into sounds, but you cannot afford to invent a fresh word every time someone reads you a number. The answer is a fixed list, worked out once: a word for every pair of digits from 00 to 99. Then 92 is always "bone", 14 is always "tyre", and a ten-digit phone number is five ready-made pictures. Fauvel-Gouraud saw the need in 1844 and printed a whole Phreno-mnemotechnic Dictionary, a classification of English words by their sounds,1 so his students could look up words for any number.

Why pairs? Ten single-digit words would take a number only one digit at a time, and a word for every three-digit number would mean a list of a thousand. A hundred pegs is the sweet spot: big enough to swallow numbers two digits at a time, small enough to learn in short daily sessions. Each peg should be a concrete thing you can see, so that it can sit on a locus in your palace and do something memorable there.

The method has been tested. In 1984 Morris and Greer showed that training in the phonetic method helped people memorise a serial list of two-digit numbers. Later experiments found the benefit is real but fragile: it depends on how well you have learned the list and on whose words you use. That is the subject of this lesson's myth check, and it is the reason the drill below gives you suggested pegs rather than asking you to invent all of them on the spot.

concepts.title: Drill: ten pegs in your palace
concepts.contentHtml:
Build the first slice of your list now, the way you will build the rest.

  1. Decode the pair. Each two-digit number gives two consonant sounds: 35 is m, l.
  2. Fill in vowels to make a concrete noun. M, l gives mule, mole, meal or mail. Pick the one you can picture most sharply; a mule beats a meal.
  3. Prefer things that act. Animals, people and objects you can make kick, smash or stink work harder in a scene than abstract words.
  4. One word, for good. Fix each word and never swap in a synonym, or you will decode "donkey" as 127 instead of 35.
  5. Place, then walk. Put each image on a locus of your first palace, in order, and walk the route once forwards and once backwards.
  6. Grow it. Add ten new pegs a day and run the whole list until each image comes to you in a second or two.
Drill Ten numbers with suggested pegs. Put one on each of your first ten loci and walk the route. The quiz will ask for the numbers in order.
  1. 14 tyre
  2. 15 doll
  3. 92 bone
  4. 65 jail
  5. 35 mule
  6. 89 fob
  7. 79 cop
  8. 32 moon
  9. 38 movie
  10. 46 roach

These ten numbers are not random. Keep them in your palace: in Lesson 5 you will find out what you have just memorised.

concepts.title: Myth check: borrow or build?
concepts.contentHtml:
Two beliefs about mnemonic systems were put to the test by Gary Patton and his colleagues.

Myth A mnemonic system works the moment you learn it.
Reality In 1987 Patton and Patrick Lantzy tried to repeat Morris and Greer's result. In their first experiment, people trained in the phonetic method did no better than untrained controls at learning two-, four- and six-digit numbers. Only when training was strengthened and recall time extended did the trained group recall significantly more. The system is a skill: a beginner fumbling for words is slower than someone just repeating digits, and the gains arrive once the list is fluent.
Myth Words you make up yourself always stick better than words you are given.
Reality Usually self-made mnemonics do win, but not here. In Patton and Lantzy's third experiment, trained people who built their own key words recalled significantly fewer numbers than controls. In 1991 Patton and colleagues found that people given ready-made code words recalled more numbers than people making their own, even after extended training, and called it an exception to the general finding. Their reading was that which source works better depends on how difficult the mnemonic is. So start from a list, and swap only the words that will not make a picture.

Wait, really? The champions use exactly these tools. Feng Wang won the World Memory Championship by recalling 300 digits read out at one per second.1 When Ericsson and colleagues tested him, he reproduced a span of 200 digits in the laboratory, encoding the digits in clusters of four,2 and they put his edge down to well-known mnemonic techniques plus training aimed at speed.3

title: Dates, Phones and PINs
description: Twain's road of kings, turning dates and phone numbers into scenes, and choosing a better PIN
tryIt: Encode one phone number you always have to look up as pegs in a single scene with its owner, and dial it from memory tomorrow.

concepts.title: How it works: Twain's road of kings
concepts.contentHtml:
Mark Twain had a problem at home. His children's governess wanted them to learn the accession dates of the rulers of England from the Conqueror onwards,1 and after days of the summer holiday they still could not hold any six of them.2 Twain knew why: the dates were all figures, and figures form no pictures. So he gave every date a place.

At the family farm a carriage road wound through the grounds below the porch. Twain measured off 817 feet of the roadway, a foot representing a year,3 from the Conquest down to Queen Victoria. At the beginning and end of each reign he drove a white-pine stake into the turf and wrote the monarch's name and dates on it. William the Conqueror was a great granite flower vase in front of the porch, labelled with his accession date, 1066.4 Henry III's 56 years became a level, straight stretch right in front of the house.5 From the porch the children could see every reign and its length at once, and they mastered all the monarchs in a day or two.6

Notice what Twain did. He laid a number line along a route you could walk, which is the method of loci from your first palace with time stretched along it. The length of each reign became a distance you could feel. You will do the same thing with pegs: the date's digits become images, and the images sit at a place, bound to the person or thing the number belongs to.

concepts.title: Drill: numbers into scenes
concepts.contentHtml:
Real numbers come attached to things: a king, a friend, a bank card. The trick is to bind the number's pegs to that thing in one scene.

  1. Split into pairs. 1066 is 10 and 66. A leftover single digit gets a short one-sound word, such as tie for 1 or pie for 9.
  2. Turn pairs into pegs. 10 is t, s: toes. 66 is j, j: judge (Fauvel-Gouraud used the same example).1
  3. Bind them to the owner. William the Conqueror stubs his toes on a judge's bench. For a phone number, put your friend in the scene, juggling the pegs.
  4. One scene per locus. A date is one scene; a long number gets one or two pegs per locus along a short route.
  5. Review. Run the scene again the next day and a few days later, spacing your reviews as you learned in How Memory Works.
Drill Twain's first eight stakes: each monarch with the year their stake marked. Turn each year into two pegs and bind them to the monarch. The quiz will ask.
  1. William I: 1066
  2. William II: 1087
  3. Henry I: 1100
  4. Stephen: 1135
  5. Henry II: 1154
  6. Richard I: 1189
  7. John: 1199
  8. Henry III: 1216

These years come straight from Twain's tape measure. He measured twenty-one feet from the vase to William Rufus,2 then thirteen to the first Henry, thirty-five to Stephen and nineteen to the second Henry, and then staked out thirty-five, ten and seventeen for Henry II, Richard and John.3 Add them to 1066 and you get every year on the card.

concepts.title: Myth check: memorable numbers
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A PIN has to mean something, like a birthday, or you will never remember it.
Reality Meaningful PINs are the ones thieves guess. Joseph Bonneau, Sören Preibusch and Ross Anderson at the University of Cambridge estimated in 2012 that guessing PINs from the birthday on documents in a stolen wallet would let a competent thief use a bank card once for every 11 to 18 wallets.1 Their advice to cardholders was to never use your date of birth as a PIN.2 With pegs, a random four-digit PIN is just two images in one scene.
Myth Some people simply cannot learn dates.
Reality Twain's children could not hold six dates by rote, then learned the whole line of monarchs in a day or two once each reign had a place and a length they could see. Rote repetition of bare figures was the problem, not the children.

Wait, really? The road outlasted the stakes. Twain wrote the essay in a Swedish village3 in the summer of 1899,4 years after the children's lesson and long after the stakes had gone, and said he could still see them as plainly as ever. Whenever he thought of an English monarch, the stakes rose before him of their own accord.5 He even noticed, he said, a foot's difference between the reigns of Richard III and James II.6

title: Pi and the Record Books
description: Piems and pegs for pi, a 154-decimal stage act, and which pi records are verified
tryIt: Walk your palace from locus 1 to 20 reciting pi to 40 decimal places, then walk it backwards from locus 20.

concepts.title: How it works: two roads into pi
concepts.contentHtml:
Time to open the envelope. The ten numbers you placed in your palace in Lesson 3 (14, 15, 92, 65, 35, 89, 79, 32, 38 and 46) are the first twenty decimal places of pi.1 Put "3." in front and walk the route: 3.14159265358979323846. You already know more of pi than most people ever will.

There are two classic ways to hold pi. The older party trick is the piem, in which the number of letters in each successive word encodes a digit.2 The best known, "How I want a drink, alcoholic of course, after the heavy lectures involving quantum mechanics", gives 15 digits and is credited to Sir James Jeans.3 Piems can run very long: Keith's "Near a Raven" (1995), a rewrite of Poe's poem, gives 740 digits,4 with ten-letter words standing for 0.5

The other road is the one you are on. Piems are fun but brittle, because every word must be exactly the right length; with pegs, any word with the right consonants will do, so the method scales. Fauvel-Gouraud used it in his 1844 lectures, promising that students would learn the 154 figures of pi in their order6 and even say which digit sat at any given place. Hérigone's cadator for 314159 was the same idea two centuries earlier.

concepts.title: Drill: the next twenty decimals
concepts.contentHtml:
Now extend the run. Decimals 21 to 40 of pi are 2643383279 5028841971.1

  1. Warm up. Walk loci 1 to 10 and recite the first twenty decimals from your Lesson 3 pegs.
  2. Add ten loci. Extend your route by ten new places in the same direction.
  3. Encode the new pairs. Use the pegs on the card below or your own, one per locus.
  4. Watch for repeats. Three pairs come back in reverse order: 79, 32 and 38 at loci 7 to 9 return as 38, 32 and 79 at loci 13 to 15. Give the returning pegs a different action at their new places (a movie on fire, not a movie playing) so they do not blur.
  5. Recite in groups. Say the digits in fours with a rhythm, checking against the card after each pass.
  6. Space the reviews. Walk the route again tomorrow and a few days later.
Drill Decimals 21 to 40 of pi as ten pairs, with suggested pegs. Place them on loci 11 to 20. The quiz will ask for them in order.
  1. 26 nacho
  2. 43 ram
  3. 38 movie
  4. 32 moon
  5. 79 cop
  6. 50 lasso
  7. 28 knife
  8. 84 fire
  9. 19 tub
  10. 71 cat

One check on your code: knife is 28, not 728. The k is silent, and you code what you hear. Lasso is 50, because the double s makes one sound.

concepts.title: Myth check: who holds the pi record?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The pi record is 100,000 digits.
Reality That is a claim, not a Guinness record. Akira Haraguchi needed more than 16 hours to recite pi to 100,000 decimal places in 2006,1 in front of witnesses in Tokyo,2 and his office videotaped the attempt for evidence.3 Guinness said he would have to make a formal claim with video and witness statements,4 and in 2012 it still had not officially verified any of his attempts.5 The record Guinness lists, checked on 1 November 2026, is Rajveer Meena's 70,000 places, recited at VIT University, Vellore, India, on 21 March 2015,6 blindfolded and in nearly 10 hours.7
Myth Pi champions are born with freak memories.
Reality This one is genuinely argued over. After testing Rajan Mahadevan, who had memorised pi, Thompson, Cowan and Frieman proposed in 1993 that he was innately endowed with a superior memory for digits and letters.8 Ericsson and colleagues repeated their tests and argued in 2004 that his digit memory came from encoding techniques learned in nearly a thousand hours of practising pi.9 Chao Lu, whom you met in Lesson 1, had a normal digit span.

Wait, really? Records move, and so do the facts around them. When Haraguchi made his attempt in 2006, Guinness listed Hiroyuki Goto's 42,195 places from 1995 as the record;10 Chao Lu's 67,890 later held the title, then Meena's 70,000. Even Haraguchi's earlier mark of 83,431 digits is dated 1995 by one news report11 and July 2005 by another.12 Check the source and its date before you repeat a record.
